title: Fewest questions to order 3 cards?
hook: Three cards, yes-or-no questions. Can a clever order of questions beat luck?

doesNotKnow: that information theory limits how few comparisons can ever work

misconception: With a clever enough method, any list can be sorted with just a few questions.
objective: The learner can say that 3 cards have 6 orders, each yes/no question at most halves them, so 3 questions are the fewest that always work, and that n items need about n log n.

claims.text: Three different cards can be in 6 possible orders.
claims.source: 3! = 6; Demo.tsx generates the six tiles by permutation. Node: permutations of 3 = 6. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): 3! = 6; node permutations of [A,B,C] = 6, same as Demo ORDERS.

claims.text: After two questions, in the worst case, two orders are still possible; the third question leaves one.
claims.source: Node script: for every asking order of A>B, A>C, B>C, answering to keep more orders gives 6 -> 3 -> 2 -> 1. Stage answers are the worst-case answers, disclosed on stage as the unluckiest ones. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): node, greedy keep-more answers for all 6 asking orders: 6 -> 3 -> 2 -> 1 every time. Reveal uses narrow([0,1]) = 2 and final 1.

claims.text: Each answer can at most halve the possible orders; two questions tell apart at most 4 and three tell apart 8.
claims.source: A yes/no answer splits a set in two, so q answers distinguish at most 2^q cases: 4 and 8. Decision-tree argument, CLRS 3rd ed. section 8.1. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): q yes/no answers give at most 2^q leaves: 4 < 6 <= 8 (decision-tree bound, CLRS 3e s.8.1).

claims.text: So 3 is the fewest comparisons that always suffice to order 3 cards.
claims.source: Node: exhaustive search over all question strategies gives optimal worst-case depth 3 for n=3 (5 for n=4, 7 for n=5); ceil(log2 6) = 3. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): node exhaustive minimax over comparison strategies: optimal worst-case depth 3 for n=3 (also 5 for n=4, 7 for n=5).

claims.text: For n cards you need about log2(n!) questions, which grows like n log n.
claims.source: CLRS 3rd ed. section 8.1: any comparison sort needs Omega(n lg n) comparisons in the worst case; lg(n!) = Theta(n lg n). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): CLRS 3e Theorem 8.1: worst case Omega(n lg n); lg(n!) = Theta(n lg n) by Stirling.

recall.question: 4 different cards have 24 possible orders. Could 4 yes-or-no comparison questions always be enough to find the order?
options: No, 4 questions tell apart at most 16 orders
recall.why: Each question at most halves the orders, so 4 questions tell apart at most 2^4 = 16 orders, fewer than 24. At least 5 are needed.
